results.label: 10B
results.summary: What the data pin down now gives a second, stricter figure for every sector, comparing each parameter's uncertainty with what its group's average alone would give rather than with the starting guess. By that measure 58% of entity parameters are informed by data, not 91%, and the input-cost pass-through and normal markup are learned for only about one entity in ten.

results.label: 7A
results.summary: Comparing sector totals with official statistics now allows for the statistic's own uncertainty, which raises the share of months inside the range from 82/100 to 92/100: Hotels employees go from 51 to 95, Hospitals employees from 62 to 100, Food utilization from 75 to 91 and Chemicals utilization from 74 to 84. Machinery production, 5.8% off, still clearly disagrees (1/100), though 9 of the 22 statistics now sit at 98-100, so the range may be a little wide.

results.label: 9A
results.summary: Data centers' overdue orders and phantom orders, which never vary, now show as fixed by the model's structure instead of a spread ratio of 1.00, so the count of quantities that come mostly from the model falls from 49 to 47. Lead time stays as it was, correctly: its copies do differ (ratio 0.999), so it really does come mostly from the model.

results.label: 6B
results.summary: Forecasts against later estimates now leaves out the 1,812 of 6,408 values whose later estimate comes mostly from the model, which moves the overall hit rate from 94/100 to 93/100 and the typical gap from 2.5% to 2.2%. The stated cause holds only for input inventory: lead time, order book and announced capacity still score 100/100 on data-informed values alone, so those ranges are simply too wide.
